# Plan: cache profile summaries in one process

## Measured problem and accepted scope
The existing profile-summary service has one active process. A one-week trace
shows repeated reads of about 900 hot keys: DB CPU is 70%, with read p95 120 ms.
Add a process-local LRU wrapper to the existing repository. Acceptance targets
are at least 60% cache hits, DB CPU below 50%, and read p95 below 60 ms, with the
existing error-rate and correctness SLOs unchanged. This is an internal backend
change with no UI, API, schema, pricing, or developer onboarding change.

## Existing contracts retained
- All reads and writes use this repository in the same process; there are no
  external DB writers. Multi-process operation remains unsupported and startup
  rejects that configuration while caching is enabled.
- Authentication and authorization run before repository access. Keys encode
  the authenticated tenant ID and validated profile ID without ambiguity.
  Values are immutable profile-summary DTOs; secrets and cache keys are never
  logged. Cached results cannot bypass authorization.
- The existing LRU adapter supports 1000 entries, a 16 MiB byte cap, and a
  30-second TTL. Recorded hot data fits those limits. Absent records use a
  distinct sentinel with a 10-second TTL; undefined means a cache miss.
- Cache operations are synchronous and atomic in the single JS event loop.
  On any cache failure the existing adapter bypasses the cache until an empty
  cache is reinitialized; repository errors keep the current typed API error
  mapping. The existing per-key
  single-flight wrapper coalesces simultaneous misses and releases on failure.
- A read already in progress when a write commits may return its earlier DB
  snapshot to that caller. Every read begun after that write completes must
  observe the committed version. TTL expiry is not a substitute for this rule.

## Proposed wrapper integration (amended by CEO review, 2026-09-09)
Keep the current read-through repository interface and shared adapters. The
original sketch (read: get, miss, DB read, set; write: DB write, delete) had no
coordination between a cache fill and a write. Review finding F1 showed that
violates the read-after-write contract above, so the ordering rules now include
a per-key fill-generation guard. These are the complete read/write ordering
rules:

```javascript
// F1: fill-generation guard. singleFlight is the existing per-key coalescer,
// extended (or wrapped) with a per-key generation and an invalidate(key) call.
async function readProfile(key) {
  if (!cacheEnabledFor(key)) return repository.read(key);          // F3: one shared flag evaluation
  const cached = cache.get(key);                                    // F4: adapter decodes the absent sentinel
  if (cached !== undefined) return cached;
  return singleFlight.run(key, async (gen) => {
    const value = await repository.read(key);                       // absent -> adapter stores sentinel (F4)
    if (singleFlight.generation(key) === gen) cache.set(key, value); // stale fill after a write is dropped
    return value;
  });
}

async function writeProfile(key, update) {
  if (!cacheEnabledFor(key)) return repository.write(key, update);
  const saved = await repository.write(key, update);
  singleFlight.invalidate(key);   // bump generation, drop the in-flight entry so later readers refill
  cache.delete(key);              // same tick as invalidate: atomic relative to other tasks
  return saved;
}
```

Accepted amendments (details in the review record below):
- F1: `singleFlight.invalidate(key)` on successful write; fill only stores when
  its captured generation is still current. Generation state lives only for
  keys with an in-flight fill, so it is bounded by concurrent misses.
- F3: `cacheEnabledFor(key)` is one deterministic function used by both paths.
  Any flag-state change (off/on or any percentage change in either direction)
  reinitializes both the cache and the single-flight state as empty.
- F4: the adapter owns sentinel encode/decode. A cached absence must produce
  the identical result the repository produces for an uncached absence. If the
  repository signals absence by throwing its typed not-found error, the wrapper
  catches only that class, stores the sentinel, and rethrows.

## Verification and rollout (amended by CEO review, 2026-09-09)
Existing repository contract tests cover tenant isolation, key validation,
absence, DB failures, and authorization. New wrapper tests cover hit/miss,
eviction and byte limits, TTL, adapter-failure fallback, successful-write
invalidation, failed-write preservation, and concurrent-miss coalescing.

Added by review (see Implementation Tasks T1-T4):
- Controlled-schedule ordering tests for the fill/write race, both the
  late-set variant and the single-flight-join variant (F1).
- Absent-sentinel wrapper tests: sentinel hit serves no DB read, expires at
  10 s, is invalidated by a create, and is indistinguishable from an uncached
  absence (F4).
- Flag-transition tests: every percentage change flushes; read and write
  evaluate the flag identically for the same key (F3).
- Bypass observability: `profile_cache_bypass_active` gauge, one structured
  log line on entering bypass naming the adapter error class and no key, alert
  when the gauge stays 1 for 5 minutes or hit ratio is below 0.6 for 15 minutes
  at 100% rollout, runbook step "flag off then on reinitializes" (F2).

The rollout uses the existing runtime feature flag: enable for 10% of keys,
then 50%, then all keys after one healthy hour at each stage. Monitor hit/miss,
eviction, cache bytes, fallback errors, bypass gauge, DB CPU, and read p95
without raw IDs. On error-rate or latency regression, disable the flag
immediately; both reads and writes bypass the cache while disabled, and any
flag-state change creates an empty cache. Cold starts remain within the
existing DB capacity. The service owner monitors the rollout and records the
results against the acceptance targets.

## Out of scope
Distributed caching, cross-process coherence, prewarming, changing consistency
semantics, or adding new product surfaces. The repository interface preserves a
future replacement path without introducing a general cache framework now.

### Step 0 outcomes
- **0A Premise:** Right problem. The trace quantifies the pain (70% DB CPU,
  p95 120 ms on ~900 hot keys). Doing nothing leaves DB headroom at 30% with
  no lever. A process-local cache is the most direct path given one process
  and no external writers. Not a proxy problem.
- **0B Existing leverage:** Reuses the LRU adapter (limits, TTL, sentinel,
  failure bypass), the per-key single-flight wrapper, the typed API error
  mapping, the runtime flag, and the repository contract tests. Nothing is
  rebuilt. Gap: the single-flight wrapper needs a generation/invalidate
  extension (F1); no existing mechanism covers it.
- **0C Dream state:**
  ```
  CURRENT STATE                THIS PLAN                       12-MONTH IDEAL
  every read hits DB   --->    read-through LRU behind the --->  same repository interface,
  1 process, 70% CPU           same interface, flagged,          cache backend swappable
                               coherent with writes               (local or shared) if a
                                                                  second process is ever needed
  ```
  Moves toward the ideal: the interface is unchanged and the wrapper is the
  seam a future backend would replace.
- **0C-bis Alternatives (D1, auto-decided):**
  ```
  APPROACH A: Inline wrapper functions in the repository module (plan's structure)
    Effort S | Risk Low | Reuses adapter, single-flight, flag
    + smallest diff, interface unchanged   - flag/cache/repo logic share one module
  APPROACH B: Decorator class implementing the repository interface
    Effort M | Risk Low | Reuses the same pieces
    + clean bypass (return raw repo when off), isolated tests   - new class, more files, same behavior
  APPROACH C: Cache at the DB query layer
    Effort L | Risk Med
    + transparent to callers   - loses the DTO-level sentinel and key contract; wrong layer
  RECOMMENDATION: A. Note: options differ in kind, not coverage. Smallest diff that
  cleanly expresses the change; B is a taste call with no behavioral gain in this scope.
  ```
  Decision: A (recommended, auto-chosen).
- **0F Mode:** HOLD SCOPE, specified by the user. No question asked.
- **0D HOLD SCOPE analysis:** Touches 2-3 files (repository module, single-flight
  helper, tests) and adds no new class. No complexity smell. Minimum change is
  the sketch plus the F1 guard; F1 is not deferrable because it is required to
  meet a stated invariant. Nothing else can be cut without breaking a stated
  requirement.
- **0E Temporal interrogation:** Decisions resolved now rather than mid-build:
  where generation state lives (F1: inside single-flight, bounded by in-flight
  keys), where sentinel encode/decode lives (F4: adapter), what "enabling
  creates an empty cache" means for partial percentage changes (F3: every
  change flushes), and who acts on bypass (F2: alert + runbook). Human ~6 h,
  CC ~45 min for the whole change.

### Section outcomes (1-11)
1. **Architecture:** 1 finding (F1). Diagram D1 below. No new coupling beyond
   repository to single-flight generation API. SPOF is the single process
   (pre-existing, documented). 10x load: 900 hot keys still fit; 100x: entry
   and byte caps evict, hit rate falls, DB absorbs the rest. Rollback: flag off
   (seconds) or revert (no migration).
2. **Error & rescue map:** 7 error paths mapped, 0 unrescued gaps after F2 and
   F4. Registry below. No catch-all handlers introduced; the only new catch is
   the typed not-found class in F4.
3. **Security & threat model:** No issues found. No new endpoints, inputs, or
   dependencies. Keys carry tenant and validated profile ID, so cross-tenant
   reads via key manipulation are not possible; auth runs before the cache.
   Memory exhaustion bounded by 16 MiB and 1000 entries. Logs exclude keys
   (F2 log line asserts this). Low likelihood, low impact across the board.
4. **Data flow & edge cases:** 1 finding (F1, async ordering). Shadow paths
   traced in D2; all handled. No user-visible interaction (backend only).
5. **Code quality:** 1 finding (F4). readProfile has 3 branches, writeProfile 2;
   no complexity concern. No DRY violation: flag evaluation is one function by
   F3. Not over-engineered: generation state is the minimum coordination that
   satisfies the invariant.
6. **Tests:** Diagram D7 produced; 4 gaps, each closed by T1-T4. 2am test: S1
   schedule tests. Hostile QA: write during coalesced fill with 50 waiters.
   Chaos: adapter throws mid-set. Pyramid: unit-heavy, correct. Flakiness:
   TTL tests must use an injected clock, not wall time.
7. **Performance:** No issues found. Hit path is one synchronous map lookup.
   Max memory 16 MiB plus bounded generation entries. No new DB queries,
   indexes, or connections. Coalescing already bounds miss storms.
8. **Observability:** 1 finding (F2). Existing metric list is adequate once the
   bypass gauge, alert, and runbook exist. Three-week debuggability: bypass
   entry log names the error class and time.
9. **Deployment & rollout:** 1 finding (F3). No migration. Flag-gated, staged,
   with explicit rollback (D5, D6). Post-deploy checklist: first 5 min watch
   error rate and bypass gauge; first hour watch hit ratio and p95.
10. **Long-term trajectory:** No issues found. Reversibility 5/5. Debt: one
    small generation API in single-flight, documented in code comment with
    diagram D3. A new engineer reading this plan in 12 months sees the invariant
    and the guard side by side.
11. **Design & UX:** SKIPPED, justified: no UI scope (internal backend change).
